newsitem.title: GREECE: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK FINANCIAL NEWS - DEC 2.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK FINANCIAL NEWS - DEC 2.

text.p: Leading stories in the Greek financial press:

--The market finds itself at the mercy of the farmers of Thessaly whose blockades of the national roads since Friday have hindered the transport of goods nationwide. Rail and road contact with northern Greece has been cut and Thessaly farmers have threatened to shut down the operation of a local airport. Farmers refuse to negotiate with ministers while the government seeks to defuse the crisis without the use of violence.

--The government's bill on tax exemptions and new taxes will be submitted to Parliament today, kicking off a week of budget-related discussions. Wednesday will see the beginning of the party discussion on the budget at the committee level, which is considered to be a barometer of the willingness of ruling party deputies to support the budget.
--The market will today be the final judge of the attractiveness of the state's new low-interest titles as the finance ministry attempts to cover lending needs of 460 billion drachmas.

--The Capital Market Commission prepares to impose penalties of fines of up to 100 million drachmas and restrictions on participation on major shareholders in some 30 listed firms for violation of stock exchange regulations. The Commission's inquiry will be completed within the week: reports say that the commission has detected violations by 55 companies.

--National Economy and Finance Minister Yannos Papandoniou turns his attention to the reform of state-run banks, following the submission of the budget to Parliament last Friday. Papandoniou is thought to be planning contacts with the heads of all banks in an effort to step up the pace of modernisation and reform in state-run banks.
--Both the development ministry - the main overseer - and insurance firms are to blame for the 'chaos' in the insurance market and the subsequent drop in consumer credibility.
--The European Investment Bank and the Greek state will sign the contract for the construction financing of the Stavros-Elefsina highway on December 16.
--Alpha Finance shows significantly improved net profits, reported at 3.5 billion drachmas, up from 2.478 billion.

--Papandoniou stressed the cutbacks in public spending when he submitted the budget to Parliament on Friday, saying that the budget would make significant inroads in the economy in the effort to meet convergence programme targets and maintain social justice. Public spending is cut back to 4.5 per cent, from 9.8 last year: this as well as a 17.5 percent increase in revenues is planned to contain the deficit.

--Certain categories of tax exemptions have once again managed to avoid being cut, making a mockery of promises for equality in the carrying of the tax burden. Those breaks that will stay include those for shipowners, pilots, and athletes.
--The 600 billion drachma natural gas investment runs into trouble as the gas reaches Greece and finds no infrastructure to allow private consumers to tap into the market.
